title: Exocrine Pancreatic Insufficiency

content_blocks.text: Syndrome that is caused by inadequate amounts of pancreatic digestive enzymes in the small intestinal lumen.
Most commonly caused by insufficient synthesis and secretion of pancreatic enzymes
In rare cases can be caused by an obstruction of the pancreatic duct or isolated lipase deficiency.

Insufficient synthesis of pancreatic digestive enzymes can be due to destruction of acinar cells resulting from chronic pancreatitis (approximately 50% of cases in dogs and almost all cases in cats) or can be due to idiopathic pancreatic acinar atrophy (PAA; most common cause of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in German shepherd dogs).
Deficient exocrine pancreatic secretion results in maldigestion and nutrient malabsorption, leading to weight loss and loose
Malabsorption contributes to small intestinal dysbiosis.

Assumed to be hereditary in the German shepherd dog and probably transmitted by a complex trait (early studies have suggested an autosomal recessive trait, but this is no longer believed to be the case).

Some dogs and cats treated with pancreatic enzyme supplements develop oral ulcerations; in most of these patients the dose of pancreatic enzyme supplements can be decreased, while maintaining therapeutic response; in a few patients, the dose of the pancreatic enzyme supplement needs to be adjusted frequently to avoid

Two cats with EPI and vitamin K–responsive coagulopathy have been reported; thus, patients that present with a bleeding diathesis should be further evaluated and possibly treated with parenteral vitamin K supplementation.
Most causes are irreversible, and lifelong
Patients with EPI alone have a good prognosis with appropriate enzyme supplementation and supportive management.
Prognosis is more guarded in patients with EPI and concurrent diabetes mellitus.
Consider EPI in young adult German shepherd dogs with weight loss and loose stools.
Do not breed animals with EPI suspected to be due to PAA.
